paper_name: DP-FAIR: A Simple Model for Understanding Optimal Multiprocessor Scheduling
paper_description: This paper introduces the DP-FAIR scheduling policy as a unifying theory for optimal multiprocessor scheduling of periodic and sporadic tasks. It provides conditions for DP-FAIR schedulers and presents the DP-WRAP algorithm, demonstrating its optimality and efficiency. The work also extends DP-FAIR to handle sporadic tasks with arbitrary deadlines.

formal_description.statement: When the total utilization of a periodic task set is equal to the number of processors, then no feasible schedule can allow any processor to remain idle for any length of time.

variables.U(τ): total utilization of task set τ

informal_sketch.intuition: If the total demand for processing time exactly matches the total available processing capacity, then to meet all deadlines, every processor must be busy all the time. Any idle time would mean less than the total required work is done, leading to missed deadlines.
steps: Consider a task set τ with total utilization U(τ) = m on m processors.
In a feasible schedule, by time t (e.g., the least common multiple of periods), the total work done by all tasks must equal t * m.
This total work is also equal to the sum of (work done by task i) for all tasks i.
If any processor were idle for any duration, the total work done by time t would be less than t * m.
This would imply that some task's deadline is missed, contradicting the assumption of a feasible schedule.
key_insights: Total utilization matching processor count is a strong condition for continuous processor activity.
Any deviation from continuous activity leads to infeasibility.

formal_description.statement: No optimal on-line scheduler can exist for a set of jobs with two or more distinct deadlines on any m-processor system, where m > 1.
assumptions: jobs with two or more distinct deadlines

informal_sketch.intuition: The presence of different deadlines makes it impossible for an online scheduler (which doesn't know future arrivals or deadlines) to make optimal decisions for all possible task sets on multiple processors. The scheduler cannot know which task to prioritize when faced with conflicting demands from tasks with different deadlines.
steps: Consider a scenario with at least two tasks having different deadlines.
An on-line scheduler must make scheduling decisions based only on past and current information.
With distinct deadlines, a decision that is optimal for one task might be detrimental to another task with a different deadline, especially on multiple processors where tasks can be distributed.
It's impossible to devise a single set of online rules that guarantees optimality for all such task sets on m > 1 processors.
key_insights: Distinct deadlines are a fundamental challenge for optimal on-line multiprocessor scheduling.
The problem is exacerbated by the presence of multiple processors.

formal_description.statement: If tasks τ are scheduled within a time slice according to DP-FAIR, and R t ≤ m at all times t ∈ σ j , then all tasks in τ will meet their local deadlines at the end of the slice.

variables.R_t: summed local utilization of tasks at time t

assumptions: R_t ≤ m for all t ∈ σ_j
formal_description.conclusion: All tasks meet their local deadlines at the end of σ_j.

informal_sketch.intuition: If the total processing demand (local utilization) never exceeds the total processing capacity (number of processors), and the DP-FAIR rules are followed, then no task can miss its deadline within the slice. The DP-FAIR rules ensure that tasks with urgent deadlines (zero laxity) are prioritized, and the condition R_t <= m prevents an overload where more tasks need to run than there are processors.
steps: A task misses its local deadline if it accumulates negative local laxity.
DP-FAIR's RULE 1 states that any job reaching zero laxity must be run to completion.
If R_t ≤ m at all times, it means the total required execution rate of all tasks does not exceed the total available processing rate.
Therefore, it's impossible for more than m jobs to simultaneously have zero laxity (which would imply R_t ≥ m+1).
This ensures that all jobs with zero laxity can be scheduled and completed within the slice, preventing negative laxity and thus missed deadlines.
key_insights: The condition R_t ≤ m is crucial for preventing overload.
DP-FAIR's priority rules (RULE 1) guarantee that urgent jobs are handled.
Local deadlines within a slice are met if the system is not overloaded.

formal_description.statement: If a set τ of periodic tasks with implicit deadlines is scheduled in σ j using any DP-FAIR algorithm, then R t ≤ m will hold at all times t ∈ σ j .

variables.R_t: summed local utilization of tasks at time t
variables.τ: set of periodic tasks with implicit deadlines

assumptions: DP-FAIR algorithm for periodic tasks with implicit deadlines
formal_description.conclusion: R_t ≤ m for all t ∈ σ_j.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma shows that the DP-FAIR scheduling rules themselves, when applied to periodic tasks with implicit deadlines, inherently maintain the condition that the total local utilization never exceeds the number of processors. This is achieved by treating idle time as a 'dummy task' and ensuring its utilization is accounted for.
steps: Introduce a dummy task T_{n+1} representing idle time, with utilization S(τ) = m - Δ(τ).
The total utilization of the augmented task set (original tasks + dummy task) is m.
The total work (including idle time) that needs to be consumed in slice σ_j is m * L_j.
At any time t within σ_j, the remaining work (including idle time) is m * (t_j - t).
The DP-FAIR rules ensure that the total work consumed by the original tasks and the consumed idle time (represented by the dummy task) matches the available processor capacity.
Specifically, the total remaining work L_t (sum of remaining work for all tasks and remaining idle time) is always equal to m * (t_j - t).
This implies that the sum of local utilizations of the original tasks, R_t, must be less than or equal to m, because the remaining idle time (S(τ) * L_j - I_j(t)) accounts for the difference.
key_insights: The concept of 'slack' or idle time as a schedulable entity is key.
By accounting for idle time, the total demand on processors is always balanced against capacity.
This lemma establishes the necessary condition for Lemma 3 to hold.

formal_description.statement: Any DP-FAIR scheduling algorithm for periodic task sets with implicit deadlines is optimal.

variables.τ: set of periodic tasks with implicit deadlines

assumptions: periodic task sets with implicit deadlines

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem combines the previous lemmas to prove that DP-FAIR is optimal. It shows that DP-FAIR ensures all tasks meet their deadlines by guaranteeing that they execute at their fluid rate and that the system never overloads.
steps: Lemma 4 proves that for any DP-FAIR algorithm on periodic tasks with implicit deadlines, the condition R_t ≤ m holds at all times within a time slice σ_j.
Lemma 3 uses this condition (R_t ≤ m) and the DP-FAIR rules to show that all tasks will meet their local deadlines at the end of the time slice.
Meeting local deadlines at the end of each time slice means that each task completes exactly its allocated workload for that slice, which is proportional to its utilization (DP-FAIR Allocation).
This ensures that each task T_i meets its fluid rate curve at every system deadline, including its own deadlines.
Since all tasks meet their deadlines, the DP-FAIR algorithm is optimal for this class of task sets.
key_insights: Optimality is achieved by ensuring tasks adhere to their fluid rates at slice boundaries.
The combination of Lemma 3 and Lemma 4 is the core of the proof.
DP-FAIR provides a sufficient set of rules for optimal scheduling.

formal_description.statement: The DP-WRAP scheduling algorithm with mirroring in odd slices will produce at most n -1 context switches and m -1 migrations per slice.
assumptions: periodic task sets with implicit deadlines
formal_description.conclusion: Upper bounds on context switches and migrations per slice.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem quantifies the efficiency of the DP-WRAP algorithm in terms of overhead. It shows that DP-WRAP, a concrete implementation of DP-FAIR, has a predictable and relatively low number of context switches and migrations per time slice, especially when mirroring is used.
steps: DP-WRAP divides tasks into segments for each processor, creating 'blocks' of execution.
Context switches occur when one task finishes and another starts on the same processor within a slice.
In the worst case, each task (except the first) might require a context switch when it begins execution on a processor.
This leads to a maximum of n-1 context switches per slice.
Migrations occur when a task's execution is split across two processors within a slice.
With the wrap-around mechanism, at most m-1 tasks will be split and thus migrate.
Mirroring in odd slices ensures that migrations happen only once per slice (in the middle), reducing the total number of migrations to m-1 per slice.
key_insights: DP-WRAP provides a concrete, efficient implementation of DP-FAIR.
The bounds on context switches and migrations are independent of task parameters, depending only on n and m.
Mirroring is an optimization technique to reduce migration overhead.

formal_description.statement: A DP-FAIR algorithm cannot cause more than (S(τ) × L_j) + F_j(t) units of idle time in slice σ_j prior to time t.

variables.S(τ): total slack of task set τ
variables.F_j(t): total slack freed in σ_j as of time t

formal_description.conclusion: The amount of idle time in σ_j up to time t is bounded.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma establishes an upper bound on the amount of idle time that can occur in a time slice for sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines. It shows that the idle time is limited by the total available slack (S(τ) * L_j) plus any slack that has been freed by tasks up to time t (F_j(t)). This prevents excessive idling, which could lead to missed deadlines.
steps: The total available idle time in slice σ_j is S(τ) * L_j.
Tasks can free slack, which contributes to the system's pool of idle time. F_j(t) tracks this freed slack.
DP-FAIR's RULE 3 prohibits voluntary idle time beyond the sum of available slack and freed slack.
The proof considers the case where mandatory idle time (due to fewer active tasks than processors) might exceed this limit.

By partitioning tasks into active (A), unarrived/slack-freeing (B), and completed (C) sets, and analyzing their processor time usage relative to their allotted capacity and the system's total capacity, it's shown that the total idle time I_j(t) cannot exceed (S(τ) * L_j) + F_j(t).
If it did, it would imply a contradiction with the task capacities or the system's ability to consume work.
key_insights: Idle time is a resource that is bounded by available slack and freed slack.
This lemma is crucial for proving that R_t ≤ m in the sporadic task case.
The partitioning of tasks and analysis of their time usage is key to the proof.

formal_description.statement: If a set τ of sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines is scheduled in σ_j using any DP-FAIR algorithm, then R_t ≤ m will hold at all times t ∈ σ_j.

variables.R_t: summed local utilization of tasks at time t
variables.τ: set of sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines

formal_description.conclusion: R_t ≤ m for all t ∈ σ_j.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma extends the R_t ≤ m guarantee to sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines. It shows that even with the complexities of sporadic arrivals and slack freeing, the DP-FAIR rules, combined with the bound on idle time from Lemma 7, ensure that the total processing demand never exceeds the available capacity.
steps: The total processor capacity consumed by time t in slice σ_j is m * (t - t_{j-1}).
This consumed capacity is composed of executed work (w_i,j(t)) and idle time (I_j(t)).
Lemma 7 provides an upper bound for idle time: I_j(t) ≤ S(τ) * L_j + F_j(t).
The total work executed by all tasks up to time t is Σ w_i,j(t).
The total required work for all tasks in σ_j is Δ(τ) * L_j.
The remaining work for task i at time t is c_i,t = δ_i * L_j - w_i,j(t) - δ_i * f_i,j(t).
The total remaining local utilization R_t is Σ (c_i,t / (t_j - t)).
By substituting the bounds and relationships, it can be shown that R_t * (t_j - t) ≤ m * (t_j - t), which simplifies to R_t ≤ m.
key_insights: This lemma is the sporadic task equivalent of Lemma 4.
It relies on Lemma 7 to bound idle time and then uses capacity accounting to show R_t ≤ m.
The inclusion of freed slack (F_j(t)) in the bounds is critical.

formal_description.statement: Any DP-FAIR scheduling algorithm is optimal for sporadic task sets with constrained deadlines where Δ(τ) ≤ m and δ_i ≤ 1 ∀i.

variables.τ: set of sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines
variables.Δ(τ): total density of task set τ

assumptions: sporadic task sets with constrained deadlines
formal_description.conclusion: The DP-FAIR algorithm is optimal for this class of task sets.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem establishes the optimality of DP-FAIR for a more general class of tasks: sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines. It builds upon the previous lemmas to show that DP-FAIR can correctly schedule these tasks by ensuring they meet their deadlines, even when arrivals are not perfectly periodic and deadlines are within periods.
steps: Lemma 3 is still applicable, stating that if R_t ≤ m, then local deadlines within a slice are met.
Lemma 8 proves that for DP-FAIR on sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines, R_t ≤ m holds for all t ∈ σ_j.
Therefore, by Lemma 3, all tasks will meet their local deadlines at the end of each time slice.
The specific challenge for sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines is handling jobs that arrive and have their deadlines within the same time slice (RULE 5).
Theorem 9 explains that RULE 5, by splitting the slice proportionally, ensures that the sub-slice capacity exactly matches the workload assigned to it.
Since the sub-slices are scheduled according to DP-FAIR (which is proven to be correct for slice scheduling by Lemma 3 and Lemma 8), the job arriving within the slice will meet its deadline.
Any other task's remaining work is also proportionally divided, ensuring it meets its deadline by the end of the original slice.
key_insights: Optimality for sporadic tasks with constrained deadlines is achieved by extending DP-FAIR's slice-based scheduling.
RULE 5 is critical for handling deadlines that fall within a time slice.
The conditions Δ(τ) ≤ m and δ_i ≤ 1 are sufficient for DP-FAIR's optimality in this context.
